en: Homage to Vajrasattva.
Having bowed to Vajrasattva and his Guru, as well as to the lineage of his sons,
the ten principles are now explained according to the sequence of the Jñānapāda school:
the protection wheel, the [main] wheel, recitation, the two consecrations, forceful yoga (haṭha), and the offering (bali).
In the *pratyaṅgira* [rite], there is the opening of the casket; the ten principles (*tattva*) are [to be visualized] in sequence.

(2) Having performed the creation of the world by means of the arrays of light rays arising from one's own seed-syllable placed on the heart, one should mentally summon the Buddhas and others before oneself by those very same [rays]. (3)
Having performed prostration, worship, confession, and rejoicing,
and having gone for refuge to the Buddha and the others, one then relies upon the path; then,
having generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), one should recollect the three gateways to liberation.
Folio missing. (i. *rakṣācakra*:
) In the intermediate directions [one should place] Ṭakkirāja, Daṇḍapāṇi, Bala, and Acala.
(2) Uṣṇīṣacakravartin is remembered as being above, and Sumbharāja below.
All the wrathful deities are born from the syllable *hūṃ*, while the Uṣṇīṣa is supreme, arising from *bhrūṃ*.
All stand in the pratyālīḍha posture upon the solar disk within the sun; their bodies are embraced by their own consorts, joined in the savoring of the bliss of innate wisdom.
Other than those from Prajñāpadmāntaka and Uṣṇīṣa, the others are proclaimed to be blue;
Prajñāntaka and the rest are white, red, and yellow, respectively. (5) [p.
Excluding Yamāntaka and Padmāntaka, those others have Akṣobhya as their crown ornament;
for Yamāri, Śāśvata is on the crown, while for the other [Amṛtakuṇḍalī], Amitābha is there.
[They hold] a mallet, a hook, a staff, a blue staff, and a lotus.
A trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, a yellow discus, and a vajra—these are the true emblems in the right hands of Acala, who has squinting eyes;
in his left hands are a discus and a noose, and he is adorned with ornaments of serpents. (7–8)
Covered by the staff-like arms of wrath, with a radiance filled with garlands of flames, it whirled in a clockwise rotation; though possessing great speed, it appeared as if motionless.
(9) The ten wrathful deities stationed upon its spokes possess great strength and prowess.
These, however, should be meditated upon as immovable, consisting of wisdom, skillful means, and bliss.
(10) Ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, the knowledge and vision of liberation, and liberation itself—these five are the supramundane aggregates. (11)
Mirror-like, equalizing, discerning, and the purity of vigor—
these ten, purified by knowledge, should be meditated upon as the well-ascertained wrathful deities for the sake of protecting the holder of the wheel from falling into the Lesser Vehicle. (12)
The *dharmodayā* seal resides within the hollow of the navel, having entered the heart of the *vajra-hūṃkāra*; therein one should meditate upon the celestial palace (*kūṭāgāra*) and so forth.
(13) (ii. Cakra)

Therein, one should visualize the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) arising from the syllable *bhrūṃ* and the wheel, born of the eternal [deity] together with his consort; it is pervaded by the sky with an expanding stream of Buddhas, endowed with squares and other [geometric forms], possessing seats of variegated lotuses upon which the moon and sun are superimposed, and adorned with all manner of exquisite jewels. 1–2.
There, upon the central seat, is the moon endowed with the thirty-two major marks and the minor signs; therein, from the heart, arises the syllable *hūṃ*.
Therefore, through the process of emanation and reabsorption, there arises Vajrasattva.
His body is like crystal or the moon; his face is blue on the right and red on the other (left);
he holds a vajra and a sword in his right hands, and a jewel and a lotus in his left.
One should meditate upon oneself as Samantabhadra, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, the glorious refuge of the world’s prosperity, radiating light in all directions.

(5) In this [mandala], all the deities, beginning with the wrathful ones, have three faces and six arms; they possess wondrous voices arising from the non-dual bliss attained through union with their own consort, the Wisdom [Bhaga]. (6)
For all [deities], there is a sword on the right and a jewel and a lotus on the left;
for those who have a lotus in the right hand, there is a gem, while for those who have a wheel, it is on the left.
For all, the right face is blue, and the face of Nīla is white.
The left [hand] of all [the deities] is white, while that of the white and black [deities] is red.
Having observed the world as a vessel to be disciplined through great passion,
one should cause the assembly of Jinas to enter within oneself by means of the sound of sexual union.
Having emanated the nine goddesses— Locanā, Rūpavajrā, and the others— through the passion for wisdom (*prajñā*), one should cause them to enter into their respective vidyās.
Again, [one should visualize] the maṇḍala arising from sexual union within the womb of one's own consort.
Having emanated the entire world here, one should cause it to enter for the sake of providing consolation.
One should enjoy [the consort] with all the Buddhas, who pervade space and arise from the melting within one's own vajra,
for the purpose of non-retrogression and for the attainment of the fruit of the knowledge of reality.
Seeing that world thus comforted, one should emit their respective seeds with these syllables—
*kṣiṃ*, *jraṃ*, *khaṃ*, *gaṃ*, *skam*— from the seed-syllable in due order.
One should [visualize] the six [bodhisattvas] beginning with Kṣitigarbha through the purification of the eyes and other sense organs.
From the seed-syllables JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ KHAṂ RAṂ, they take on the forms of Rūpavajrā and the others;
and by means of these syllables LĀṂ MĀṂ PĀṂ TĀṂ, they are of the nature of Locanā and the rest. || 14–15 ||
From the seed-syllables BUṂ ĀṂ JRĪṂ KHAṂ HŪṂ, the Buddhas, whose forms consist of the aggregates and so forth,
[emerge]. OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ— thus the mind, radiant and interlaced by the two arms,
enters the interior of the secret lotus and, out of passion, melts away.
Through that great passion, both wisdom and means have become fluid;
one should recollect the goddesses with the verses beginning "O Vajra," while perceiving the fluid state as a calamity due to the requirement of rising from it.
Through the perception of reality as being like an illusion, from that melting [of the seed-syllable], Mañjuvajra himself arises from the sword produced by the seed-syllable *maṃ*.
He has the form of saffron, with a blue face at the base and white on the right, while the other [faces] are red. || 19–20 ||

Having the form of a youth's ornament, uniquely beautiful with the bliss of wisdom, he has two arms embracing the true Prajñā, and holds the face of his own radiant Prajñā. His hands hold a shining sword, an excellent arrow, a blue lotus, and a bow.
Having accomplished the three worlds through the emanations of the spreading flood of Buddhas,
one should meditate on Akṣobhya— either black or born from a *vajra* produced from the syllable *hūṃ*— in the center.

In this universal maṇḍala, one should meditate upon the Leader according to one’s wish. Arising from attachment to existence, he is infinite; yet through attachment to tranquility, he partakes in misfortune.
Having cultivated service through illusion, he becomes the very essence of the dharmadhātu.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the intrinsic essence of the dharmadhātu.
Through the arising of the fruit that is the outflow from the limbs of gentle service,
the *ālayavijñāna* with its outflows ceases, and the *ādarśajñāna* (mirror-like wisdom) comes into being.
[The lords are] Kṣitīśa, Vajra, Ākāśa, Lokeśa, Skambha, and Bhadra.
Having filled the eyes and other sense organs with the seed-syllables, one shall attain omniscience.

(26) The Bodhisattvas everywhere manifest in the forms of Śāśvata and the others, bearing their respective marks and belonging to their respective families; the accomplished one, however, is the form of Vajrasattva. (27)
By means of the factor of gentle cultivation, which is conjoined with the fruit of maturation,

one should generate the wisdom of equality and thereby turn back the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas). The welfare of the world proceeds through the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, and the Emanation-body.
Therefore, one should emanate the empowerment of the secrets of mind and so forth as a limb of the sādhana:

from the *hūṃ*, *āḥ*, and *oṃ* born of the true lords situated in the moons at one’s own heart, throat, and head, located in the centers of the vajra, lotus, and wheel, and possessing the seed-syllables residing in the signs at one’s own heart. (29–30)

Having meditated on that, through the rays of light from its seed-syllable, one should worship the Lords situated in the directions by means of the forms of Rūpavajrā and the others; then, one should request their empowerment by means of the verses beginning with "Cittavajra" for those who possess the three vajras.

Having caused the requested Citta-vajra and the others to enter into one's own mind and so forth, one should become possessed of the ego-identity of that [deity] by means of the mantra beginning with "Oṃ sarva... and so on. 32
When that [practice] is mild as a limb of the sādhana, human effort is possible;
and conceptual construction is exhausted by the moment of the arising of discernment.
Above the Mind-Vajra, the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva) is considered to be like the pledge-being (samayasattva).
Born from the sign of his own seed-syllable upon the moon, with his heart marked by the sign of his own seed-syllable,
he impels the Lords situated in the directions with the light from the heart of the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva).
Then, by means of the Vidyās arising from that radiance, [he is consecrated] with the waters of nectar from the filled jars.
The illustrious Lord Kuleśa, having been consecrated, becomes the Diadem (Makuṭa).
When the fruit called "purity" has arisen from the Great Accomplishment (Mahāsādhana),
the active consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna) is exhausted due to the occurrence of the performance of duties.
Likewise, one should purify one's own innate wisdom (prajñā) through the [five] outflows and so forth, as well as the intermediate [stages].
At her head, heart, navel, and secret place, and at her feet,
one should visualize these as individual atoms, using the seed-syllables Oṃ, Hūṃ, Svā, Āḥ, and Hā, which consist of the families of Śāśvata and the others.

Having filled the *karṇikā* of the excellent lotus with the five *sambuddhas* and *hūṃ āḥ*, and having thoroughly purified [it], one should cause the Buddhas to be impassioned by means of that [lotus] with the *hūṃ* of the excellent vajra:
*oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. (39)

Having established within oneself the mandala of Buddhas pervading the sky— marked by the moon in the heart and possessing the radiance of the heart— and having generated the host of Jinas from their respective seed-syllables therein and rendered them stable, [one should contemplate] that which has the nature of pure consciousness, situated upon a vajra-lotus. (40)
One should emit [the deities] according to this rite for the purification of ignorance within the worlds.
Having exhorted the Lord Akṣobhya, the Jina who accomplishes the purpose of great hatred,
one should visualize the Lord of the Vajra as Vajradhṛk, possessing the luster of a sapphire.
Having withdrawn it into himself, the illustrious one should establish it within all phenomena.
And with "Jinajik," he should contemplate the primordial light, the Jina who effects the purpose of great delusion.

Having dismissed the Lord who bears the discus, one should meditate upon Ratneśa within the orb of the full moon; he is yellow and possesses equal vigor. Having dismissed him, one should visualize the one with the face of Kumāra in the southern direction.
One should visualize Vāgīśa, known as Ārolika, the Lord who effects the purpose of great passion,
red in color and holding a lotus, seated upon a sun-disc on one's back.
One should visualize Amogheśa, known as Prajñādhṛk, who bestows the purpose of generating great passion and jealousy.
One should meditate on the one who wields the sword, greenish-dark in hue, from the northern sun.
All [the deities] wear matted hair and crowns, and are adorned with all ornaments. Regarding the eternal leader and the others, they are led by that leader from the mandala.
Having projected that form into himself, the skillful one should withdraw it as before.
Then, he should again meditate upon Akṣobhya as the leader in each respective place.
Furthermore, Moharatī is in the southeast, and Locanā has the luster of the Lord of the Body (Agni).
Dveṣarati is in the southwest, [the consort of] Cittesha and Candramāmakī; Rāgarati is in the northwest, [the consort of] Vāgīśa and Pāṇḍarā;
and Vajrarati is in the northeast, known as Tārā, like Ratneśa.
The wheel, the divine red lotus, the yellow lotus, and the blue lotus—these are declared to be their emblems in sequence; the remaining [emblems] should be assigned as for their respective lords.
[They are located] in the four corners starting from the southeast, and on both sides of the eastern gate.
The manifestations of body and so forth, through the three principles (*tritattva*), are known as Rūpavajrā and the others.
A mirror, a lute, perfume, elixir, clothing, and the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) are considered their respective symbols in sequence. (53–54)
Seated upon moons, wearing jeweled crowns, and joined with their own consorts as the means (upāya),
these goddesses— who embody non-dual compassion— are adorned with all varieties of ornaments. (55)
At the eastern gate is Yamāntakṛt, seated in the wrathful posture (krodhaparyaṅka), resplendent with the form of Citteśa;
he is the destroyer of epidemics and the annihilator of the aggregates and the objects of knowledge.
At the western gate is Aparājita, terrifying with fierce eyes like those of Kāyeśa.

"Prājñāntakṛt" (the ender of higher knowledge) is the destroyer of desire through the abandonment of the afflictions of self-view; he is the destroyer of the mass of evil—death and birth—and is Aśvakandhara at the posterior gate. "Padmāntakṛt" (the ender of the lotus) is the destroyer of perception, known as Vāgīśa and Abhoga. || 57–58 ||
Akṣobhya, the destroyer of fierce obstacles, is in the north, and Amṛtakuṇḍalin is at the gate;
they are known as Vighnāntakṛt due to the purification of the Kriyā-sura and others.
They have furrowed brows, hair blazing upward, and brown hair, eyebrows, beards, and eyes; their mouths are turned back, their tongues are lolling out, and they laugh fiercely with bared fangs.
All these wrathful deities possess solar discs and shine with the brilliance of the sun;
their hands hold a vajra, a mallet, a staff, a lotus, their own vajra, and so forth.
Their bodies are adorned with fierce serpents, and they are embraced by their respective consorts.
They should be meditated upon as having short bellies and hanging breasts, possessing the vision of the three mandalas, and non-dual.
Having beheld the perfected wheel through the state of the mass of bliss,
one should [invite] the Buddhas, who have been gathered by the wisdom-wheel, from the seed-syllable in the heart by means of hooks.
Having offered water for the *argha* and other rites that has been consecrated with mantras and mixed with flowers from the directions beginning with the moon,
one should place that wheel upon the [mandala] wheel, which is presided over by the eye, body,
and so forth.
One should meditate upon that [deity] as being sprinkled as before, according to the degrees of outflow (*niṣyanda*) and so forth, up to the highest degree.
The Vajra-holder is on the crown of the Buddhas; the others are sprinkled by their own lords.
Having sealed the cause with the fruit, one seals the fruit with the cause.
The gatekeepers are considered to be Kāyeśa, Akṣobhya, Vāgīśa, and Citteśa.
(65) Having thus sprinkled [the offerings], one should [visualize] form and the other [sensory objects] entering within the lotus of wisdom by means of the light from one's own heart,
as a city [of deities] arising from the pores of the skin through Rūpavajrā and the others.
Having worshipped oneself and the lords of sages, one becomes the embodiment of the worship of those worthy of worship:
*Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra-worship of all Tathāgatas.*
One should praise the wheel in its own form with the verses beginning "Akṣobhya" and so forth.
One should meditate on the vajra, arisen from the syllable *hūṃ*, situated in the intermediate space. One should place within it the nectars marked with the syllable *oṃ*. (67–68)
Heated and purified by the wheel of downward-moving wind and fire,
the supreme vajra is brought down and unified by the rays of the syllable OṂ.
Having meditated on it as being filled with the nectar of gnosis, one should visualize the tongue as a vajra marked with the syllable HŪṂ.
One should satisfy the entire wheel situated within the moon of the heart by means of that [offering].
At the time of eating as well, the adept should thus prepare his own food;
[he should do so] with the Lords created from its rays, free from all improper mental constructs.

Having made the world consist of the Buddha-nature, one should cause it to enter within the seed-syllable in the heart. Having meditated upon one's own mind as radiant, situated within the center of the heart-symbol (the lotus) in the form of the moon and the heart-bindu, one should cause the Jñānasattva to shine forth. || 72–73 ||
Having visualized the vajras of mind, speech, and body, as well as the *samayasattva* and the mandala, by means of a garland of radiating light rays; 74.

Through withdrawal, one should meditate upon her in the heart as she flows with the nectar of perfect knowledge, fulfilling the needs of the world through the arrays of light radiating from every pore.

(75) Having meditated on the circle of sages (*municakra*), which arises from the tip of the nose of the Vidyā, resides within its own subtle sign, is self-cognizable, and contains all deities in their entirety;
and having seen the emanation [of light] issuing from its rays as a cause for stability, (76)
One should perform it with various signs of the Buddhas, or otherwise not at all.
By duly pouring down the cloud of the water of the true mind, moistened by the moon and the *praṇava* upon the head, one should effect the gratification of body, speech, and mind. (77–78)
Having thus rested, performed the recitation (*japa*), and dismissed the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*), he—
having established the true wheel through the three principles (*tritattva*) and bearing the pride of the Lord—
beheld the entire world as liberated through this vision of reality (*tattvadṛśā*).
Having made a vow here out of compassion and for the benefit of others,
the adept, in the form of Vajrasattva, should perceive all phenomena and conduct himself accordingly.
Even during the intervals between sessions, having fully emanated the maṇḍala from the three principles (tritattva), he should remain so.
Having performed worship, recitation, and so forth, he should proceed as before.
Having risen in the morning as before, the beginner should perform the ritual.
One who has attained some degree of immersion in knowledge should instantly take hold of the mandala.
One should recite [the mantra] untiringly during the junctions of the day, presiding over the eyes, body, and so forth.

When the yogin has attained some degree of mastery over that which is perfectly accomplished in all its aspects and performs the processes of emanation and reabsorption, he should constantly rely upon yoga. || 84–85 ||
Meditating with right knowledge as his sword, he should bring about the welfare of the entire world.
Having thus visualized the true wheel and having obtained the very sign, || 86 || [p. 197]

Having performed the recitation according to the rules while stationed in the wheel—whether requested by himself or by another, or while striving for the sake of others, or desiring spiritual accomplishment—he should write [the mandala].
He should recite the mantra of the Wheel-Lord one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), and likewise ten thousand (*ayuta*) for the others.
The seed-syllable should be infused with the three principles (*tritattva*), or the emission (*utsarga*) should be performed in that same manner.
Just as the wheel has been meditated upon, so too should the maṇḍala be drawn.
However, in this case, at the place where the deities reside, one's own respective insignia should be drawn as prescribed;
specifically, at the location of Locanā, the eye should be drawn by the wise.

The first person should perform it himself; the second likewise should do so while in a state of lunar purity (*vidhu*); the third, being skillful, should construct the mandala through the power of divine possession (*āveśa*). Having brought a boy and a girl into possession during the twelfth year, he should worship them.
The wheel that one might accumulate through those two [offerings] is not equal to that of the former practitioners.
For one who has attained mastery over knowledge should indeed create the mandala by means of the mind alone;
because through its empowerment, the wheel is seen by both oneself and others.
The reality of the wheel and the deity is now being established:
because of its squareness and lack of inequality, due to the equality of the awakened and the unawakened;
and because of the impossibility of the multiplicity or unity of body, speech, mind, and phenomena. (94)
The mindfulness directed toward that, as well as the faith therein, is considered the gateway to awakening;
from that,
there follows the abandonment of past and future distortions and their non-arising.

Likewise, for the sake of the arising and stability of the truth that has not yet arisen, there is vigor; and therein, the vigor by which [one acts] is here the "door of speechlessness. Desire, vigor, mindfulness, and wisdom are the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
The mindfulness that exists toward these [objects] constitutes the western gate here;
moreover, it consists of the faculties and powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Furthermore, the two—concentration and wisdom—constitute the twelfth, the upper gate.

The first dhyāna has five factors: with applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), born of seclusion, and consisting of joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha). The second [dhyāna] has four factors: without applied and sustained thought, and characterized by internal serenity (adhyātmasamprasāda). 100
Mindfulness arises from clear comprehension, happiness, equanimity, and one-pointedness of mind;
the third [dhyāna] also has five factors, including the feeling of pleasure and pain.
Through mindfulness and equanimity, there is purity, and the fourth [dhyāna] is born of seclusion.
The eastern gate and the others are considered to be formed by the four meditations (dhyāna) previously mentioned.
Śūraṅgama, Khagañja, Vimala, and Siṃhajṛmbhita—with these, which encompass all [qualities], there should be a pedestal (vedikā) on all sides. 102–103.
Therein is the assembly of those who hold the scriptures and so forth, intent on performing worship;
for they possess diverse ornaments because they fulfill the hopes of the world.
They have shaken off [defilements] through discipline, uphold the true Dharma, and are perfected in the purity of their voice with its eight qualities.
It resounds with the bells of the banners at the tops of all [the towers], stirred by the wind.
The "necklace" (hāra) is the removal of the afflictions (kleśa), through the abandonment of all afflictions.
The "Half-Necklace" (ardhahāra) is known as that which removes half of the afflictions (kleśa).

The garland (srak) is the purity of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), while the mirror (darpaṇa) is by means of the "mirror-like" [wisdom]. Furthermore, the seven factors of enlightenment are: the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya) and mindfulness (smṛti).
Through the application of concentration, joy, vigor, equanimity, and pliancy;
and because the fly-whisk is a royal insignia, it represents the Buddha’s knowledge of the path.
The unsurpassed bodhicitta is naturally luminous and pure.
The moon mandala is said to be produced from the welfare of all sentient beings;
likewise, it consists of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*) and is born from the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).
The sun mandala is said to be the great light of the illumination of liberation.
The food offering consists of the dharmas, while modesty, shame, and restraint constitute the lamps, flowers, incense, and perfumes found within the mandala;
likewise, well-sung songs, dance, and instrumental music [are included], because they increase great bliss. (111)
The wheel is beautifully adorned with pillars through the purification of the eight liberations (vimokṣa).
Because it sets in motion the Vajrayāna of the Buddhas of all directions and the three times,
it is praised as being surrounded by a circle of vajras, perfectly circular on all sides.
The colors are the five perfectly awakened ones, because they delight sentient beings through their respective gnoses.
The full vases are the natural outflow of the completion of the accumulations, due to being moistened by compassion.
The city is so called because it is the city of liberation, and the maṇḍala because it gathers together the essential [reality]. (114–115)

From the purification of the great hatred of the aggregate of consciousness (jñānaskandha) into the dharmadhātu, Akṣobhya arises; through that very purity, there is the purification of the lotus and the vajra. From the purification of form and the great delusion (mahāmoha) into the mirror-like [wisdom], Śāśvata is remembered.
Ratnasambhava arises from the purification of pride regarding the equality of sensations;
Amitābha from the contemplation of the aggregate of perception as great passion; and Amoghasiddhi from the great envy toward the formative forces of the performance of duties. || 117–118 ||
Locanā is characterized by emptiness, the gateways, the elements, compassion, and skillful means;
Māmakī by the signless, great loving-kindness, water, and the vow;
and Pāṇḍarā by fire, the vow, joy, power, and the mind. (119)
Through knowledge, equanimity is free from volitional effort, and by means of the wind, one is delivered.

(120) By means of the purity of the six perfections—giving and the rest—which oppose the adversaries such as stinginess, Rūpavajrā and the others are to be meditated upon. Through the purity of faith, Yamāntaka is [meditated upon], having abandoned the obscuration of the aggregates and the conceit of self-existence arising from lack of faith. (121)

Through the abandonment of the affliction of laziness, as well as the Māra of the view of extremes and the obscuration of the afflictions, the one endowed with vigor here is the Destroyer of Wisdom (Prajñāntaka). The mindful one, who destroys the lotus and brings an end to false views, death, and birth, is to be meditated upon as [Padmāntaka]. (122–123)
The accomplished one, who destroys the karma of distraction caused by the adherence to views of gods,
should be meditated upon in the form of Samādhi as the destroyer of all obstacles.
Through the purification of the six perfections beginning with generosity, all deities possess six arms;
through the purification of the three liberations, they attain the form of three faces.
The wise know that profundity arises from the purity of emptiness, while magnificence arises from compassion.
All [the mandalas] are blissful, consisting of wisdom and means, both profound and vast.
(126) Likewise, the purification of the signs of the painted mandala is performed through their purification.
Having recognized the wheel produced from colored powders as complete in every respect, (127)
One should cause the host of Victors to enter within oneself by means of the sound of the vajra-lotus.
Having visualized the wheel arising from the lotus of wisdom as before,
one should then expand that wheel and cause it to enter the circle of dust.
Having brought [the deities] into the wheel of wisdom (*jñānacakra*) and having offered the water for honor (*argha*) and so forth as before,
one should effect their entry and so on with *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ* by means of Yamāntaka and the others.
Then follows the consecration of the eyes, the body, and so forth, and once again the offering of the water for honor and so on.
Having praised, prostrated, gratified, recited [mantras], and meditated, one should satisfy [the deity].
(131) Having worshipped the guardians of the directions situated in their respective positions, one should enter the mandala.
(132) Having become a conqueror of the three worlds, and having obtained ornaments and garments as appropriate, [one should proceed].
Having performed the circumambulation and bowed to the wheel, one should complete [the rite] with a fire offering (*homa*).
Thus is the accomplishment of the wheel; now the dismissal (*visarjana*) is described.
Seated at the eastern gate or other locations, the preceptor (*ācārya*), being well-composed, [should proceed].
Having performed the threefold meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through the secret and other forms of worship,
and having made the offering, one should partake of the nectar and then offer praise.

Having brought forth the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) and then dismissed it, [one should contemplate] the commitment (*samaya*) as being non-obstructive and blissful in every respect, having the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
"Oṃ! You have accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings; having granted the desired accomplishments (*siddhi*), go now to the realm of the Buddhas, and may you return again!

One should cause that [wheel], beginning with the vajra of body and mind, to enter one's own body and so forth. This is the sequence for those [deities] drawn upon the walls of ruined stūpas and the like.

Having uttered the mantra beginning with the syllable *muṃ*, one should scrape away the colored powder (*rajas*) with the vajra. One should cause the great sound to flow forth, preceded by songs, instrumental music, and so forth.
Some maintain that the reality (*tattva*) of the wheel and the deity is indeed distinct;
thus it is designated as both the protection-wheel (*rakṣācakra*) and the [main] wheel.
(iii. *japa* / *jāpa*:
) Now, the explanation of what was previously mentioned as "recitation" (*jāpa*) must be stated; thus it is said. Regarding that, it is stated in the *Tantra* for the purpose of recitation:
"This placement (*nyāsa*) extending up to the threefold vajra is called the 'three vajras'."
A threefold radiation should be performed in the presence of body, speech, and mind.
Having meditated upon the root— the body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas— [one should perform it].
This firm method of awakening should be performed with the vajra of knowledge.
Reciting it, one should emanate the vajras; at the conclusion, one should enter into withdrawal.
By means of this vajra of recitation, one becomes equal to the mind of the three vajras.
Recitation (japa) is declared to be speech; all that is spoken by the voice is called mantra.
Mantra, mantra is said to be the utterance that impels the reality (tattva).
Whatever arises dependently through the senses, their objects, and the mind—
That mind is declared to be "manana" (contemplation), and the syllable *tra* is for the purpose of protection (*trāṇa*).

By means of the threefold division—namely, within one's own deity at the heart, throat, and head, extending as far as the vajra situated in the center of the vajra-lotus-cakra—it is called the "placement of the three vajras" (*trivajra-nyāsa*), meaning the placement of the three vajras. Alternatively, the collection of the three vajras is called the "three vajras. Or else, "extending as far as the vajra" means that the placement should be performed up to the placement of the Jñānasattva. "The threefold radiation should be performed" refers to [the radiation] from the moon-disks at the hearts of the Body-Vajra and the others.

The instruction is as follows: at the time of reciting the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, the Body-Vajra and so forth are to be emanated; at the time of reciting the seed-syllable situated upon the moon in the heart of the Jñānasattva, that [seed-syllable] itself is also to be emanated. Regarding this, according to the instruction, having placed them within the mandalas of Wind, Water, Indra (Earth), and Fire, one should emanate the Body-Vajra, Speech-Vajra, Jñānasattva, and Mind-Vajra respectively at the time of reciting their own mantras. Others, however, say it refers to the seed-syllables alone. "In the proximity of body, speech, and mind" means from the mantras of body, speech, and mind.

Others, however, believe [the emanation] arises from the seed-syllable of the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) alone. Some, moreover, describe the radiation of seed-syllables situated within a single lunar disc. Having meditated upon the body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas, there is the "supreme worship of the Buddhas" by means of the "gnosis-vajra," which is non-referential gnosis (*nirālambanajñāna*). According to some, the form-vajras (*rūpavajra*) are to be radiated from the gnosis-being. "While reciting, one should radiate the vajras" means that at the time of recitation, one should radiate the vajras of the body and so forth from the body-vajra and others, together with the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*).
"At the conclusion" means "at the time of withdrawal"; that is, at the completion of all recitation, one should enter into or perform withdrawal together with the *apāna* wind. As it has been said:
"While reciting, one should emit the mantra through the *prāṇa* winds, withdrawn by means of breath-extension (*āyāma*).

By this "vajra-recitation"—meaning that the recitation itself becomes a vajra when performed without attachment and without objective apprehension—one [becomes] equal to the mind of the three vajras, either through the sequence of vajra-recitation or by being identical in essence to the mind of the three vajras, characterized by equality, during the state of recitation or the state of fruition. This was stated by the Blessed One in this very context:
The vajra-recitation is great wisdom, characterized by the indivisibility of the three bodies;
through the meditations on the indivisibility of the three vajras, the wisdoms of the Buddhas are attained.
By means of recitation and the application of the vajra, one is empowered by all the Buddhas.
Thus it is said. It is also stated in the *Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra*:
"In the heart, throat, lips, tongue, palate, and likewise in the head;
internally, externally, and in between the two."

[205] “But the mere phenomenon alone is the word *jāpa*, which is also non-reliant. He explains the meaning of the term *jāpa*: “*Japa* is whispering; the meaning is that *jāpa* is internal or external muttering. However, for those who see reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), everything is indeed mantra; thus he says, “all speech is called mantra. He explains the meaning of *mantra*: “*Mantra*, *mantra*—it is the incitement and the speaking of reality; or it is a designation based on convention or a cause. This was said by the Blessed One:
The mantra is said to be an invocation because it brings [the deity] face-to-face;
just as some great person, when summoned by the force of sounds,
arrives upon merely hearing them, so too does [the deity] come from the moment of recitation.

Thus, by means of that which consists of both reflection (*manana*) and protection (*trāṇa*), he declares the mantra’s nature to be that of *bodhicitta*. "Whatever... whatever"—that is, because it is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), it is a reflection; its determination is through emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As it has been said:
"That which is dependently originated [is devoid of intrinsic nature].
And it has been stated again:

"That which is dependently originated, they declare to be emptiness"—this is the meaning of the syllable *ma*. Regarding the syllable *tra*, it is for the purpose of protection (*trāṇa*). Protection means that by means of it all sentient beings are saved; compassion is its meaning, and thus the sound *tra* [expresses] that. Therefore, according to the principle that "bodhicitta is traditionally known as the inseparable unity of emptiness and compassion," bodhicitta is the ultimate mantra. This is because, while it consists of syllables, it is designated as such either by way of indicating that [ultimate reality], or because it is ultimately non-different from it, or because it takes that form as its object. Recitation of this kind is called "neuter recitation" (*napuṃsakajāpa*).
Regarding this, it was said by the Blessed One in this very context:
206] "The reality of the three-vajra commitment belongs to those who possess the commitment-vajra."
That very [recitation] of all vajras is called the "neuter recitation.
This was stated by the Blessed One in this very [text]:
"The reality of the three-vajra commitment is the middle [commitment] of those who possess the commitment-vajra."

"That alone is the recitation (*jāpa*) of all *vajras*, and it is not considered neuter. The "triple-vajra commitment" (*trivajrasamaya*) is the form of the object of focus for the deities who are indivisible from body, speech, and mind. "Reality" (*tattva*) refers to its reality as well: wisdom (*prajñā*) whose mode is non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). That itself is the "middle," the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*), because it is free from the positions of existence and non-existence. "Of the Samaya-vajrin-s" refers to the deities of the delusion family (*mohakula*); this is their recitation in this manner. As it has been said:
"Passion is the woman, hatred is the man, and delusion is that which is devoid of both."

Thus, he extends this same recitation (*jāpa*) even to the recitation of all the Tathāgatas, stating: "That very [recitation] belongs to all Vajras," or alternatively, "to the Samayavajrins. And he says that this very [recitation] is the recitation of all the Tathāgatas. Regarding the phrase "that very": or rather, the connection is that "this very [recitation] is the recitation of all Vajras for the Samayavajrins. Some say that because there is an absence of conceptualization regarding female or male, the recitation is neuter. At the time of recitation, the Blessed One speaks of emanation (*spharaṇa*) by way of another method: "Alternatively, emanation should be performed according to each [deity] through the threefold division."

Therein, at the time of uttering the syllable *oṃ*, one should emanate the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*)—residing upon the wind-maṇḍala and empowered by the three vajras (*oṃ āḥ oṃ hūṃ*)—and then worship it by emanating the Form-Vajra (*rūpavajra*) and so forth; finally, one should withdraw it. Then, regarding the water-maṇḍala, one sees *oṃ āḥ āḥ hūṃ*. At the beginning of the utterance of the syllable *āḥ*, and so forth, it is as before.

In the Māhendra [mandala], some say that the seed-syllable of the Jñānasattva is "Oṃ Āḥ Maṃ Hūṃ" and so forth, according to its own nature. Likewise, in the fire-mandala, one should visualize the seed-syllable of Cittavajra as "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Hūṃ. Thus, the recitation should be performed through the previously mentioned deity-yoga. This is the reality of recitation (*japatattva*).
[Page 208] (iv. Secret Initiation)

Now the consecrations (*sekāḥ*) are explained. Regarding the term "consecrations," the two consisting of the secret and the wisdom [consecrations] are specified because they are primary; these two alone are presented as the nature of reality (*tattva*), since the others are subordinate members of these and are external by way of purifying the body. In that regard, the mantra-practitioner who has received the initiation of the *vidyā*, being faithful, having properly propitiated the true guru, and having prepared a [consort] who possesses the heard rules and so forth, who is youthful, aged twelve years or more according to the divisions, and adorned with all ornaments, and having placed her to the left of the guru—

Having worshipped the Guru, who possesses wisdom, with various offerings, and having performed the mandala circle and other rites, the mantra-practitioner—seated upon a couch or similar bed that is pleasing to the mind in a secluded place adorned with various offerings, within a mandala drawn with colored powders or upon a cloth mandala at one of its sections—should entreat the Guru with secret verses for the sake of the secret initiation: "By the grace of your feet, I have attained the unsurpassed practice;
now, O Lord, grant your favor through the jewel of initiation. (1)
Just as the Lord of Great Bliss revealed to the Buddhas, the Protectors, that which is called the pure reality, so too, O Protector, be gracious to me! O Lord,
deliver me from suffering, from the abode of all miseries.
Show compassion toward those who are helpless, which cuts through all suffering.
O Lord, apart from your lotus feet, I have no other refuge.
Therefore, be gracious, O foremost of Buddhas, hero of the world, great bliss!
Thus,
having heard that supreme and divine procedure for the formal request,
the illustrious Guru, an ocean of virtues, gave rise to compassion for his disciple.
Having become serene of face, compassionate, and joyful,
one should cause [the disciple] to hear the divine vow, the supreme secret distinction:
"O son, you may kill living beings, and you must speak false words."
You must take what is not given, and you must consort with the wives of others.
O gentle one, you must maintain the supreme vow of the consciousness;
likewise, feces, urine, meat, blood, and the fifth, which arises from the mind.
And the lamp of cows, horses, and so forth, according to the rules of purification and the like,
must be consumed by you constantly; this is the most wonderful samaya.

Then the preceptor, situated in the midst of the entire circle of deities, having cast the five nectars and so forth into the lotus of his own vidyā, and having thoroughly empowered the Prajñā—who is of the same nature as himself and endowed with yoga—through the yoga of the non-duality of wisdom and means; and having emanated various rays of light from the heart of his own Jñānasattva, established all sentient beings in the innate bliss of great happiness; and by that very sound of union, having summoned all the Tathāgatas through his mouth and caused them to melt with the passion of supreme great bliss;

Having identified and stabilized the innate (*sahaja*) according to its respective locations through the distinctions of Ānanda and so forth, and having retained it as long as possible by means of the *phaṭ*-sound, the wind, and so on; and having focused the disciple in the form of Vairocana or his own chosen deity, and having empowered the eyes, body, and so forth; one should cause that mind—which has descended via the vajra-path and reached or not yet reached the lotus of one's own goddess—to fall into the mouth of the disciple by means of the *Nāma* and *Jyeṣṭhā* [mudrās]. Some say it is by means of the *vajra* itself being pressed by those two.

Then the disciple, possessing the yoga of the deity, saying "Oh, what bliss!", should partake [of the substance], resolving with conviction: "This is the supreme nectar that dispels the darkness of all ignorance. Some say that it should likewise be given by the wisdom consort (*prajñā*). This is the state of consecration for all Vajras, *raṃ*;
all Vajras and the extensive arrays of the foremost rites are accomplished. (10)
Thus concludes the secret initiation.
(Now follows the wisdom-knowledge initiation:
Then, having taken that which arises from the mind, together with flowers, situated within the lotus—

Having caused the disciple to grasp the vajra with his own mouth for the sake of worship and with the mouth of the Vidyā, the Guru then requests his own [consort]. Then, the Guru, empowered as before, [empowers] that woman or the maiden.
Holding the hands one above the other, one should dedicate the vidyā within that [mudrā].
"This delightful dhāraṇī of yours is to be cultivated; it was devised by the Buddhas.
By means of the application of the sequence of wheels, experience true bliss."
Through contact with wisdom, the illustrious one should clearly perceive reality;
while seated in the vajra posture, he should observe the mind as it enters within the jewel.
Thus it is said.
Then that worthy woman should proclaim the vow to him:
"O Vajrin, are you able to consume feces, urine, and so forth?"
"Tell me, O Vajradhara, what is the great bliss of blood, semen, and likewise flesh; the supreme devotion of women, and the kissing of the lotus of the womb?
Then the Blessed One, the Vajradhara, smiling, spoke this:
Moreover, O Goddess, I cannot bear the consumption of semen, blood, and the like;
rather, women should always practice devotion through kissing and the sexual organ itself.
She, with her excellent organ uncovered, should show her own lotus in its true nature. 18–19.
"Aho! My lotus is endowed with all happiness;
for him who serves it according to the ritual, I stand before him.
This is the pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the liberator of the realm of sentient beings."
The King, who is himself Great Bliss, is established within all phenomena.
That which is the space in the center of the *bhaga*, adorned with the five voids,
endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and embellished by eight petals—
Situated there, it constantly flows as the nectar in the form of drops.
He commands it:
"Attain liberation! Hoḥ!"

Then, having correctly discerned that channel of Vajradhātvīśvarī through the word of the guru and by means of non-dual union with wisdom, he should slightly stimulate it with his finger and further with a tongue-stick. (23)
That channel, which conveys supreme sexual bliss, attains full expansion when the Lord of the Elements has entered the practitioner who possesses the wheel of his chosen deity.
Seated upon a comfortable seat and concealed behind a cloth or similar screen, the Guru,
having beheld the disciple— who is illumined by the rays from his own heart and impelled by the light of the seed-syllable of the Buddhas—
[should consecrate him] with excellent jars filled with the water of wisdom, with the nectar-water of the vajra-lotus.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with the Rūpavajrī and others, one should cause him to enter therein.

Then, by the instruction of the Guru, the disciple too should emanate sentient beings as much as he desires, perceive the bodhicitta, and having emitted it, take it up himself with his tongue while it rests in the lotus and drink it. "One should give it from the mouth of the Prajñā into one's own mouth. Then, requested by them for suitable offerings and fees, the Guru—having placed his two hands upon their left hands as before while they are both seated in the utkuṭuka posture—should place his right hand upon their heads; this is the Vidyā-vrata.

"From this day forward, I have properly given this maiden to this practitioner for the sake of attaining great awakening; may the Tathāgatas take note of this. This delightful dhāraṇī of yours is to be cultivated, as ordained by the Buddhas. (27)
Buddhahood is not attained by any other means, and these three worlds are pure.
All phenomena are non-dual, yet they are characterized by the appearance of duality; therefore, you must not effect separation from this [nature] within saṃsāra. (28–29)
"This is that unsurpassed vidyā-vow of all the Buddhas;
for the fool who transgresses it, there shall be no supreme accomplishment.
Thus one should bestow the vidyā-vow. * * *
(vi. Haṭha:

Now, that which was briefly mentioned as "haṭha" is explained in detail. "Haṭha" refers to the means of achieving haṭha. In this regard, a yogin who possesses the yoga of the three samādhis, who is intent upon the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*) according to the prescribed method, and who abides by the commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*), should, having obtained the causal sign (*nimitta*), practice for six months in a cave on Mount Añjana or a similar location.
If it is not accomplished, then once again, remaining established in the pledges (*samaya*) and so forth according to the unimpaired ritual procedure, one should meditate for eighteen months.

If it is still not accomplished, then at another junction of time (*sandhyā*), one should begin the practice of forceful yoga (*haṭhayoga*). The practitioner of Vairocana is black; possessing non-dual yoga with his well-practiced wisdom, surrounded by black mandala deities, he should meditate on the moon-seat and the rest of the peaked temple as black, according to the rite for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).

Then, having performed the worship, praise, and tasting of the nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), one should cause the Tathāgatas drawn by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the heart to descend into the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyayoga*). Having produced the maṇḍala-circle within the fire-maṇḍala in the form of the visualized maṇḍala-circle—trembling and terrified—one should again melt the host of Tathāgatas drawn by the flames of light-rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart through the yoga of wisdom. Having emitted them through the path of the vajra, another self-lord (*svādhipa*), likewise black and wrathful, emerges with a vajra and seizes [the victim] by the neck with his left hand.

Taking the vajra-mallet held in the right hand and striking it upon the head of the Yamāntaka-kila while reciting the mantra with urgency and wrath, one should nail down the wheel situated upon the lotus. The mantra is:
*oṃ āḥ chinda 2 hana 2 daha 2 dīptacakraṃ vairocanavajraṃ kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ*.

And one should visualize that stake being pressed down by the vajra; thus success (siddhi) occurs. And this success consists in remaining within the form of the maṇḍala-circle until the end of existence for the sake of performing the welfare of sentient beings. Following this principle, the forceful practice (haṭhasādhana) of those belonging to that family should also be understood in this way. Likewise, this very same procedure applies to the practitioners of Amitābha and those of his family. However, for the stake of Raktapadmāntaka, as well as the stake-mantra, it is different:
*oṃ āḥ hrīḥ bhūr bhuvaḥ*. [One should meditate on] Amitābha or the other [deity].
*Kīla hūṃ phaṭ hūm*. [p.
213] This same procedure applies even for the practitioners of the families of Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, and Amoghasiddhi; however, the *vighnāntaka-kīlaka* mantra is different.
Oṃ, O King of Jras, nail down Akṣobhya or whichever other [deity] there may be! Hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ!

For those who [place] Vajrasattva upon their crown as well, this very procedure applies. Furthermore, this forceful practice (*haṭhasādhana*) will not succeed if performed for only eight days or up to a fortnight. And the entire ritual must be performed by means of non-apprehension (*anupalambhayoga*), with power, fearlessly, and through the application of the pin, the one being pinned, and the pinner; otherwise there is no success. Thus ends the forceful practice. (vii. The Offering: *bali*)

Now the offering of the *bali* is explained. In this regard, the sequence for the reality of the *bali* is as follows: the yogin, instantly appearing as the circle of his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) in black color, draws in all the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) from the ten directions with rays of light from the heart of wisdom and pins them down. Therein:
In the eastern direction is Indra, whose mount is an elephant, blazing with ornaments; he is yellow, mounted upon the white Airāvata, and holds a thunderbolt in his hand. (1)
To his left is Kṛṣṇa Viṣṇu, mounted upon Garuḍa;
he holds a mace and a discus in his right hands, while on the other side he carries a conch and the Kaustubha gem.
Then, in the south-eastern quarter, there is Agni, red and corpulent, seated upon a goat and holding the Abhaya mudrā and an eye.
Dwarfish, with a crown of matted hair of a tawny-brown hue, he holds a staff and a water-pot in his left hand.
In the south is Kṛṣṇa, fierce with a bright red torch, threatening with his staff;
King Yama is mounted upon a buffalo and adorned with garments and ornaments.
In the southwest is Asita Kravyād, resplendent with a garland of beards.
Naked, with a mouth formidable with fangs, deformed, and with hair disheveled;
holding a small knife and a skull-cup, he is fierce, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a corpse.
In the western quarter is Varuṇa, white, seated upon a serpent and holding a serpent-noose.
In the northwest is green Vāyu, seated on a deer and wearing garments of wind;
in the north is yellow Nakulī, Kubera, who is borne by men.
He holds a citron in his right hand, and Vināyaka is at his left.
Seated upon a mouse, Śita holds a sweetmeat ball, a spear, and a root;
in the northeast, Īśāna is mounted on a bull and holds a trident;
he is white, his body adorned with a skull, and he wears a tiger skin at his side.
His left hands hold a khaṭvāṅga, a ḍamaru drum, and a skull-cup;
above him are the Sun and Moon, red and white respectively, standing upon their chariot.
And Brahmā, yellow in color, stands upon a swan, holding a lotus in his right hand—these indeed [are the deities].
Brahmā, wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavītin), holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and a staff (akṣadaṇḍa).
Vemacitrin is below, black in color, standing upon a chariot and holding a sword.
To his left is Pṛthvī, yellow in color, seated upon a lotus and holding a golden pitcher.
Having meditated upon all the lords of the directions situated in the upper, lower, cardinal, and intermediate directions,
accompanied by their retinues, one should drive in the ritual stakes (kīla) in this sequence.

One should emanate from the seed-syllable in one's own heart the ten excellent wrathful deities mentioned in the *Rakṣācakra*, in the form of stakes below the navel and in their natural forms above it; having emanated them, one should nail down the lords of the directions with another emanated wrathful deity. (14)
Oṃ āḥ Yamāntakṛt, nail-pierce all the wicked Indras and Upendras together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ Prajñāntakṛt, nail-pierce all the wicked Yamas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ Padmāntakṛt, nail-pierce all the wicked Nāgas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ! Vighnāntakṛt, nail down all the wicked Gaṇapatis and Kuberas, together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ!
Ṭakkirāja, nail down all the wicked Agnis, together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ!
Nīladaṇḍa, nail down all the wicked Nairṛtis, together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ Mahābala, nail-pierce all malevolent winds together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ Acala, nail-pierce all malevolent Īśvaras together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, nail-pierce all malevolent Candrapitāmahas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ āḥ sumbha! Nail down all the wicked ones, Vemacitrin, and the Earth-deity with their retinues—hūṃ phaṭ!
Beginning from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet, these [beings] are again nailed down by the yogin of the knowledge of equality regarding the nailing-stakes (kīlaka).
Thereupon, all the assembly members become three-faced and six-armed. 15.

On the moon is Vajrāyudha, yellow in color and holding a vajra; to his left is Māyāvajra, blue, holding a mace and a discus, seated upon a lotus on the sun. In a triangle is Vajrāgni, standing on the sun, with matted hair, and Śakra, holding the gesture of fearlessness and an eye. (16–17)
Then follows the white Vajrakāla, stout, holding a water-pot and a staff;
and the donkey Śūra, standing upon a spear, brownish-brown with eyebrows, beard, and hair, and holding a staff.

Stationed on the sun, Vajramusala is black; he holds a katṭārikā and a sword, while in his left hands he holds a skull-cup and a jewel. Akṣobhya is upon the crown of his head. Nāgavajra is white and stands upon the moon; he holds a snake-noose and a sword.
Green in color, he holds an unerring [arrow] in his left hand; on the moon [disk], he wears armor of vajra-fire.
Vajrabhairava is golden-hued, holding a citron, a sword, and a wheel;
in his left hands, he holds a lotus and a *nakulikā*; he stands upon the sun and bears Akṣobhya as his crown ornament. || 20–21 ||
Seated upon the moon, white in color, he holds a sword and a water-pot in his right hands, and a jewel and a vessel of liquor in his left; he bears Akṣobhya as his crown-ornament.
Seated upon the moon, he is considered to be the Vajra-krodha, white in color and wearing a crown of Amitābha.
Holding a trident and a sword in his right hands, and a jewel and a wheel in his left;
on the moon [disk] is Vajraprabha, white in color, with a speech-vajra crown, his supreme hands resplendent with a lotus, a sword, a jewel, and a wheel. || 23–24 ||
Ratneśa, with the crown of [Aksobhya], is red upon the sun and wears a vajra earring;
Maunavajra, with the crown of Kāyeśa, is yellow upon the moon.
The earth is like Maunavajra, and these three bear their respective symbols upon the moon.
Vemacitrin, Aruṇakṛṣṇa, Akṣobhyāṅka, and Vajravān—
[these four] all sit in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, with their six arms embracing their respective consorts.
In the right [hands] of all is a sword, and in the left, a lotus and likewise a jewel.
The application of light with their respective faces, as well as their own seats upon the universal lotus;
furthermore, their emergence from the first letter of their names joined with the *anusvāra*.
Alternatively, after the ritual of pinning (*kīlana*), all [deities] hold their own emblems in their right hands.
On the crown is Vajrasattva, and by the remaining [deities], they are like Vajrasattva.

217] Then, having set aside the previous yoga and performed the yoga of one’s own chosen deity, one should offer [the oblation] accompanied by the five offerings according to the number of syllables in the name of the object of devotion and so forth, and provided with parasols, banners, musical instruments, and the like. Even in their absence, visualizing them as such, and having produced them in the form of nectar preceded by the water for welcoming (*argha*) and other offerings, one should present them to those [deities] with this mantra:

Oṃ Āḥ! All you lords of the ten directions, residing within the atoms of all the world-systems of the three times and ten directions—namely: Vajrāyudha, Māyāvajra, Vajrānala, Vajrakāla, Vajramuṣala, Nāgavajra, Vajrāṇila, Vajraśauṇḍa, Vajrabhairava, Vajrakrodha, Vajraprabha, Vajrakuṇḍali, Maunavajra, and Vemacitrin; and the Earth Deity with her retinue: accept this offering of the bali-oblation provided with flowers, incense, perfumes, food offerings, and so forth, and enjoy it for my sake.

Subjugate, paralyze, and destroy all obstructors and Vināyakas who steal away my gold, fine gold, wealth, grain, life-span, youth, health, and true happiness; subjugate, paralyze, and destroy all wicked and malicious humans and non-humans! For the increase of my gold, fine gold, wealth, grain, life-span, youth, health, happiness, and great bliss, until the limit of the seat of enlightenment, bring them to me! Be my helpers! Grant me peace and protection! HŪM!

Then, having performed worship with the Rūpavajrā and others emanated from the seed-syllable in the heart, and having offered praise with the verses beginning with "O Akṣobhya," and seeing them pleased, one should ask for forgiveness with this:
"Oṃ Āḥ! The syllable A is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen; Hūṃ Muḥ!"
The Bali offering.
(viii. Bhāvyapratyaṅgirā:

Regarding "Pratyaṅgire," there are two types of Pratyaṅgirā: Bhāvyapratyaṅgirā and Pratyaṅgirā. Among these, Bhāvyapratyaṅgirā is as follows: that very same protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*), when visualized rotating counter-clockwise and adorned with the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin and the Vajra-Hūṃkāra situated in its center, becomes the Pratyaṅgirā wheel. Visualizing that very wheel, the yogin, preceded by offerings and the like, should worship it after reciting the mantra three times.

Oṃ āḥ! O Uṣṇīṣacakravartin! Whatever mantra, tantra, yantra, ritual applications (*prayoga*), and so forth have been performed by anyone for my sake—cut them all! 2! split them! 2! accomplish them! 2! shatter them! 2! burn them! 2! cook them! 2! cause them to tremble! 2! destroy them! reduce them to a hundred thousand fragments! 2! O Uṣṇīṣacakravartin! *Bhrūṃ* 3! *Hūṃ* 3! By reciting this three times at night and during the day, whatever person intends harm toward a practitioner, all of that falls back upon that very person. This is the Bhāvya-Pratyaṅgirā. (ix. The Lekhya-Pratyaṅgirā)

For the sake of protection or for the pacification of obstacles, one who possesses the yoga of Vairocana should, according to the rules, [draw a mandala] upon birch bark or similar materials for the benefit of men; however, for women, it should be square with four gates, using *gorocanā* (bovine gallstone).

Having drawn a circle of the earth provided with four gate-towers and so forth, one should draw within it a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) with twelve prongs; in its hub, an eight-spoked wheel; and in the center of that, the syllable *ha*, topped by a triangle and endowed with a crescent moon and a drop (*bindu*) as its crest. Having written inside that: *oṃ āḥ jinajik [name] śāntiṃ kuru hūṃ*, one should write the emission mantras (*utsargamantra*) of Akṣobhya and the others in the directions starting from the east, and the emission mantras of Locanā and the others in the directions starting from the southeast, on the wheel.

On the rim, one should write: *oṃ āḥ phala phala tiṣṭha tiṣṭha [name]'s upadravādikaṃ bandha bandha hana hana daha daha amṛte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, wrapping it with a clockwise rotation and drawing it with the head [of the mantra] facing inward. At the gates starting from the east, one should write the *utsarga* mantras of Yamāryā and the others; and for the six goddesses beginning with Rūpavajrā, one should write their respective seed-syllables, such as *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* or *jaḥ* and so forth, each in its own place. Having wrapped the tube with gold or other materials possessing the eight qualities, and having had the *vidyā* (mantra) inscribed with lac, vermilion, and so forth, one should consecrate it.

Then, the master, possessing the yoga of the three samādhis, having visualized within the heart of his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) the wheel described immediately above as being situated inside the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), complete with the mantras representing the nature of the twenty-one deities beginning with Vairocana according to their respective positions, and with all calamities and so forth destroyed by the array of Noble Amṛtakuṇḍalin produced from the rays of light from each individual syllable of the garland-mantra placed upon the rim; and having accomplished the object of attainment (*sādhya*) produced from the first syllable of its own name at the navel of that wheel; and having brought forth that gnosis and unified it [with himself];

Visualizing his vajra-body armored with the *haṃ* syllable as a coat of mail, and seeing that body being pervaded by a stream of nectar flowing from the garland of emanation-mantras of Vairocana; [visualize it] consecrated by an empowerment of white-colored nectar-pitchers through the arrays of white-colored deities emerging from the mouths of light-rays, or consecrated by the entry of oneself into the state of melting through the bodhicitta born of union. Meditating thus on [the body] as free from all defects, one should repeat the mantra again and again.

Then, having performed worship, one should wear [the amulet] placed within a casket such as a small box upon the body, the neck, or other parts, in the location of the deity. From that, peace (*śānti*) arises;

and in rites for pacification (*śāntika*), all ritual actions whatsoever are included, because the rite of pacification consists essentially in the quelling of all undesirable defects. Thus concludes the written *Pratyaṅgirā*.
(x. *puṭodghāta*):
This is designated as *puṭodghāta*.
[It applies to] one who harms the Three Jewels and one who is intent on betraying the guru.
He who would always kill his mother, his father, and even the noble ones—
toward such a person, the Lord, the Master of Yoga, whose mind is overcome by compassion,
would pray for the turning away from those deeds through gifts, honors, and other means.
But the fool does not persist [in this]; at that time, he should undertake this rite:

having performed yoga during the interval between the twilight periods, he should instantly expand the streams of all Buddhas through the mudrā practiced with the radiance from the heart of the Jñānasattva.
By that very ray of light, the one to be subdued is drawn forth and placed before him.

Then, with that [ray] grasped as a weapon, one should visualize all the multitudes of Buddhas and even ordinary people being cut into pieces, pulverized, and destroyed by that cruel-minded one with harsh words. Seeing that wicked being—who, thinking "I am a slayer of many Buddhas," is filled with remorse, terrified by the fear of hell, and without refuge—one should generate compassionate wrath for the sake of rescuing him and confess that deed exactly as it was committed to one's own Lord.
Whatever action has been performed by him, and whatever is being done by him now,
that is being seen by you, O Lords who act for his benefit;
for were there no remedy for this, he would become fuel for the Avīci hell.
"O Greatly Compassionate One, I shall perform this as a yogin only with your permission.
Therefore, O Vajrin, grant me leave for this ritual act."
"Otherwise, you yourselves would be the transgressors of the pledge here.

Having heard their acceptance, he became enraged toward them; then that Lord Nīla, together with his retinue, uttered the sound of a command beginning with: "Let all the hosts of obstacles listen!"—"Let all the hosts of obstacles residing in body, speech, and mind listen!"
I am the glorious Vajradhara, the one who employs the wheel of command.
With my vajra of blazing form, I shatter those born of the three bodies;
if anyone should transgress against me, they would be shattered—of this there is no doubt.

Having meditated on the ritual procedure without obstruction, with the intention of benefiting all sentient beings, by means of the arrays of wrathful deities radiating from the *ājñācakra* and pervading the sky;
[he visualizes] those born from the sound of the vajra-lotus uttered by the Perfectly Awakened Ones drawn forth from his heart and hands.

The skillful practitioner, enraged at the form of Sumbha who holds a noose, a goad, an arrow, a jewel, and a sword, should cause the protection and the offering for the sādhya to be drawn forth by means of those [rays] emanated from them:
*oṃ āḥ he sumbha, attract the protection and so forth of [the person named] amuka! jaḥ hūṃ!* 12.
Above is BAṂ and below, in the region of the forehead, is the universal vajra (viśvavajra) produced from the final vowel, marked with HŪṂ.
This constitutes the outer protective enclosure; having drawn it forth, it is held on the left.
Then Sumbha was again made to enter by way of the vajra-path;
he stood face-to-face before the Jñānasattva Akṣobhya.
Śrī Sumbha should entreat the Jñānasattva with many arguments:
"Since you are in every way established in such an action, it is proper for you to abandon it for the sake of future welfare. (15–16)
This man is devoid of devotion, a slayer of the Buddha, and a reviler of his gurus;
therefore, he now forfeits both protection and empowerment.
This is so unless you yourselves are liars regarding your own words.
"And those who violate the samaya"—by this [statement], he consented, saying, "Do so.
Then, satisfied by these arguments, he abandoned his objective and departed;
immediately, together with Samputa, he brought Sumbha there.
Whatever kind of *sampuṭa* was brought forth, that is now described here:
the vajra, the sword, likewise the lotus, the jewel, and the wheel, in their proper order.
Having worshipped them according to reality as they reside within the upper and lower *sampuṭas*, then—

Having cast [the mantra] into the lotus of the deity’s mouth, which shines with its [lips] joined like a casket, one should again contemplate it as being situated therein. The Perfect Buddhas, drawn forth by the seed-syllable of the heart, emerge having become liquefied.
With that [mantra] in the form of a stake for the enemy of obstacles, one should stake everything:
*Oṃ āḥ gha gha ghātaya 2 sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ kīlaya 2 sarvapāpān phaṭ vajrakīla vajradhara ājñāpayati amukasya jñānasattvaṃ kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ*.
Then, the object of practice (*sādhya*) is situated in the southeast mandala directly in front.

One should visualize him as anointed with oil, naked, unprotected, devoid of luster, overwhelmed by fear, lacking any defense, and with disheveled hair. Then, by means of the flame from his heart, one should cause the Buddhas to enter into one's own body.
[The world is filled] by the Fully Awakened Ones themselves, who have been emanated in forms that are formidable, fierce,
and terrifying, appearing as hosts of violent wrathful deities bearing sharp swords and other weapons.
One should see [the enemy] cut into pieces, slain, and likewise ground to powder;
[then] a supreme, certain bad rebirth [awaits him].
If it is known with certainty that an action is about to be performed,
then even its contradiction is inconceivable, because knowledge and action are [thus] understood.
Thus concludes the procedure for the opening of the casket.
May that person who has correctly understood the ten principles become one by whom [the truth] has been attained through the withdrawal of those ten principles.
